title: Ordered SQL Patterns,Islands and Completeness
description: Derive daily islands,precise event sessions,calendar gaps,all-required membership and latest-per-group results with explicit identity,tie and missing-value policies.

questions.question_text: What is the input grain for a daily-streak calculation here?
questions.explanation: Repeated same-day events do not represent additional active days.

questions.question_text: What does the date-minus-row-number anchor identify?
options: Consecutive daily runs within a learner partition
questions.explanation: A missing day changes the derived anchor.

questions.question_text: How many active days are in April 1, April 2, April 2 after deduplication?
questions.explanation: The repeated April 2 contributes one daily identity.

questions.question_text: Why partition the row numbering by learner?
options: Different learners must not share a streak sequence
questions.explanation: The streak belongs to one learner’s date population.

questions.question_text: Under the stated session policy, what does an exact 30-minute gap do?
questions.explanation: Only a strictly greater gap starts a new session.

questions.question_text: Why compare seconds against1800 rather than truncated complete minutes against30?
options: A 30-minute-one-second gap must start a new session
questions.explanation: Complete-minute truncation could conceal the one-second excess.

questions.question_text: What supplies a deterministic tie-breaker for equal event times?
questions.explanation: The complete order makes the event sequence reproducible.

questions.question_text: Does a short cross-midnight gap split the session automatically here?
options: Yes, every SQL session ends at midnight
No, the policy uses elapsed time only
questions.explanation: Calendar-day splitting would be an additional explicit rule.

questions.question_text: What is needed to report dates with no activity?
questions.explanation: Absent dates must be supplied before the optional activity join.

questions.question_text: Where can a filter accidentally remove calendar gaps?
options: A null-rejecting WHERE predicate on the optional activity side
questions.explanation: Logical filtering after null extension can defeat preservation.

questions.question_text: What does double NOT EXISTS express for required exercises?
options: No required exercise lacks a completion witness
Every completion must be unique by amount
Only the highest exercise identifier matters
questions.explanation: It implements an all-required relationship test.

questions.question_text: What is the universal-logic result for an empty requirement set?
options: Every candidate satisfies it unless an extra guard is required
questions.explanation: Product rules can add a nonempty-configuration requirement explicitly.

questions.question_text: Why can COUNT equality fail for relational division?
options: Duplicate or unrelated completions can inflate counts
questions.explanation: Counting must preserve the required relationship identity and scope.

questions.question_text: Which ranking chooses one deterministic latest row?
options: ROW_NUMBER with timestamp and stable tie-breaker
RANK on timestamp only with all ties
questions.explanation: The one-row requirement needs a complete selection order.

questions.question_text: Which ranking can retain all latest timestamp ties?
options: ROW_NUMBER with a unique identity always
RANK using only the intended timestamp peer order
questions.explanation: Adding the unique identifier to peer ranking would break the tie.

questions.question_text: When should approved eligibility be applied for latest-approved selection?
options: Only after choosing the latest unrestricted row
questions.explanation: A rejected newest row must not hide an earlier eligible winner.

questions.question_text: Does CTE syntax guarantee a particular physical materialization?
questions.explanation: Logical decomposition and physical plan are separate.

questions.question_text: Can a late event change derived session numbers?
options: No, derived labels are permanent by definition
questions.explanation: A recomputation can merge or split the historical partitioning.

questions.question_text: What remains separate from a correct fixture result?
options: Performance, provider and operational history guarantees
questions.explanation: A frozen result check establishes only its tested contract.

questions.question_text: What is the session partition for 09:00, 09:30, 10:00:01, 10:10 here?
options: First two together, last two together
questions.explanation: The1801-second middle gap starts the second session.

coding_problems.title: Find consecutive active-day islands
coding_problems.task: Return learner_id, first_day, last_day, active_days for each consecutive daily run. Deduplicate learner-date pairs first. Order by learner_id, first_day.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE learner_activity(event_id INT PRIMARY KEY,learner_id INT NOT NULL,activity_date DATE NOT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT learner_id,activity_date FROM learner_activity),numbered AS (SELECT learner_id,activity_date,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY learner_id ORDER BY activity_date) AS rn FROM days),anchored AS (SELECT learner_id,activity_date,DATE_SUB(activity_date,INTERVAL rn DAY) AS island_key FROM numbered) SELECT learner_id,MIN(activity_date) AS first_day,MAX(activity_date) AS last_day,COUNT(*) AS active_days FROM anchored GROUP BY learner_id,island_key ORDER BY learner_id,first_day;
hints: Subtract the row number in days to form a stable island anchor.
coding_problems.explanation: Consecutive dates advance together with their row number, keeping a common anchor. A missing date shifts that anchor.

coding_problems.title: Sessionize events with an exact thirty-minute threshold
coding_problems.task: Return event_id, session_no for each learner event. A learner’s first event starts session 1; a gap strictly greater than1800seconds starts another session. Equal timestamps use event_id order. Order output by learner_id, event_time, event_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE practice_events(event_id INT PRIMARY KEY,learner_id INT NOT NULL,event_time DATETIME NOT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: WITH previous AS (SELECT event_id,learner_id,event_time,LAG(event_time) OVER(PARTITION BY learner_id ORDER BY event_time,event_id) AS previous_time FROM practice_events),marked AS (SELECT event_id,learner_id,event_time,CASE WHEN previous_time IS NULL OR TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND,previous_time,event_time)>1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous),sessions AS (SELECT event_id,learner_id,event_time,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY learner_id ORDER BY event_time,event_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS session_no FROM marked) SELECT event_id,session_no FROM sessions ORDER BY learner_id,event_time,event_id;
hints: Use LAG before the cumulative boundary sum.
coding_problems.explanation: The1801-second middle gap begins session 2. Each learner starts their own sequence.

notes:
## Derive the pattern from a precise business question

Advanced SQL patterns combine familiar operations into reusable reasoning techniques. Gaps and islands identify consecutive runs, relational division tests whether all required relationships exist, greatest-per-group selects qualifying extremes, and sessionization partitions an ordered event stream. These names describe families of solutions rather than magic templates. Each requires explicit identities, ordering, missingness and boundary policies before a query can be judged correct.

Imagine a training service recording learner activity dates and timestamped practice events. A streak report asks for consecutive active dates. A session report groups events separated by no more than thirty minutes. A completion report asks whether a learner completed every required exercise. Although each report uses related activity data, its grain and notion of completeness differ. Write that distinction beside the query instead of adapting a convenient pattern by changing only table names.

## Deduplicate daily activity before finding islands

For a daily streak, one learner can have several events on the same date. Those events represent one active day under this requirement. Deduplicate learner_id and activity_date before numbering; otherwise multiple events can create false boundaries. Use DATE columns or a deliberately chosen local-date conversion. A UTC timestamp crossing midnight can belong to another calendar day in the learner's reporting zone, so time-zone policy is part of the input contract.

For sorted distinct dates, subtracting an increasing row number from each date produces a stable grouping key within a consecutive daily run. In MySQL, a DATE_SUB expression can use the row number as a day interval. Group by learner and that derived anchor, then compute the first date, last date and number of active days. A missing date moves the anchor and starts another island.

```sql
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT learner_id,activity_date FROM learner_activity
), numbered AS (
  SELECT learner_id,activity_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY learner_id ORDER BY activity_date
         ) AS rn
  FROM days
), anchored AS (
  SELECT learner_id,activity_date,
         DATE_SUB(activity_date,INTERVAL rn DAY) AS island_key
  FROM numbered
)
SELECT learner_id,MIN(activity_date) AS first_day,
       MAX(activity_date) AS last_day,COUNT(*) AS active_days
FROM anchored
GROUP BY learner_id,island_key
ORDER BY learner_id,first_day;
```

Dates April 1, April 2 andApril4 form runs April 1–2 with two active days and April 4 alone. A second April 2 event does not extend the first streak because deduplication already fixed the grain. Missing or NULL dates need an explicit policy; the exercise schema excludes NULL dates rather than pretending an unknown date occupies a position in the calendar.

## Find session boundaries with LAG and an explicit threshold

For timestamped events, order each learner's rows by event_time and a stable event_id tie-breaker. LAG supplies the previous event time. Mark the first event and each gap strictly greater than thirty minutes as a new session. A cumulative sum of these boundary markers assigns a session number. An exact thirty-minute gap stays in the same session under this policy; changing greater-than to greater-than-or-equal changes the result.

Measure gaps in a unit that preserves the threshold precisely. Comparing TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, previous_time, event_time)>1800 avoids the truncation surprise of comparing complete minutes when a gap is thirty minutes and one second. Fractional-second inputs need a compatible precision policy. Define whether a calendar-day boundary also splits sessions; the worked exercise uses elapsed time only and can keep a short cross-midnight gap in one session.

A cumulative window should state ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW over the complete deterministic order. Equal timestamps are peers by time but still separate event identities. A stable identifier makes their processing reproducible. Session numbers are derived report labels, not permanent business identifiers safe to store indefinitely while older events can arrive and renumber history.

## Fill calendar gaps without confusing absence and zero

A report needing every date requires a calendar population, not merely grouping observed events. A bounded recursive CTE can generate dates between explicit endpoints, or a reviewed calendar dimension can provide them. Left join activity summaries to those dates and apply the intended zero policy for absent counts. A missing measurement can remain unknown when the domain distinguishes it from a confirmed zero.

Bound recursion and validate the start/end relationship. A malformed interval should not become an unbounded date generator. Predicate placement matters: filtering the optional activity side in WHERE can remove the very empty dates the calendar was meant to preserve. Aggregate to date grain before joining when raw events would multiply another independent reporting branch.

## Express all-required membership with relational division

Suppose required_exercises lists the exercises needed for a certificate and completions records learner-exercise relationships. A double NOT EXISTS asks whether there is no required exercise for which the learner lacks completion. Duplicate completion rows do not manufacture extra requirement coverage because existence is a witness test. A raw COUNT equality can be wrong when duplicates or unrelated exercise completions inflate the numerator.

The empty requirement set needs a decision. Under universal logic, every learner satisfies all requirements when none exist. A product may instead forbid issuing a certificate with no configured requirements; that additional guard must be explicit. NULL relationship keys and incomplete ownership scope also deserve attention. Use declared identities and trusted eligibility rather than comparing display names.

## Choose greatest-per-group tie behavior deliberately

A latest-submission report can require one deterministic submission per learner or every submission tied at the latest timestamp. ROW_NUMBER over descending submitted_at plus submission_id can choose one row. RANK using only the timestamp can retain all top timestamp peers. Including submission_id in the ranking order would break those peers and change the all-ties requirement.

Filter eligibility before ranking when only approved submissions belong in the comparison population. Ranking every submission and then removing a rejected winner is not equivalent to choosing the latest approved submission. Test a learner whose newest overall row is rejected and whose earlier row is approved. A NULL timestamp requires a stated ordering or exclusion policy rather than a guess from the current engine's default.

## Preserve grain when composing patterns

One row per active day, one row per event, one row per session and one row per learner completion are different intermediate grains. Name each CTE according to its role and project its stable keys. A join between session rows and raw daily events can multiply totals if their relationship is not one-to-one. DISTINCT on a final measure can hide some duplication while discarding legitimate equal-valued facts.

Break a large query into independently checkable relations and predict each fixture's intermediate rows. CTE syntax improves readability but does not guarantee one physical materialization or a particular performance improvement. Inspect the actual plan and representative execution before claiming a pattern is faster than another correct formulation. Correctness comes first; execution evidence remains engine-specific.

## Test boundary cases and late data

For islands, include duplicate dates, a missing middle date, two learners and one isolated day. For sessions, include an exact threshold, a one-second-over gap, equal timestamps and a cross-midnight short gap. For division, include duplicate evidence, an unrelated exercise and an empty requirement set. For latest-per-group, include ties, rejected newer rows and a learner with no eligible submission.

Late-arriving events can merge previously separate sessions or extend an earlier streak. If a downstream system persists derived session labels, it needs a recomputation/versioning policy. A report query returning correct current labels does not establish stable historical identifiers. Keep the operational contract separate from the deterministic calculation on a frozen fixture.

## Solve two ordered-pattern exercises

First exercise: return daily islands for each learner after deduplicating activity dates. For April 1, April 2, April 2 andApril4, the solution has a two-day first run and a one-day second run. A separate learner on April 2 remains in a separate partition. Explain the anchor calculation and why counting raw events would report the wrong streak length.

Second exercise: sessionize events at 09:00, 09:30, 10:00:01 and10:10. The first two share session 1; the last two share session 2 because the middle gap is 1801 seconds. Add two same-time events and retain their stable event identifiers. Continue with [window frames](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/window-navigation-frames-and-distributions), [recursive CTE safety](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/cte-hierarchy-safety-and-plans) and [NOT EXISTS](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/not-exists) to connect ordering, calendar populations and completeness witnesses.
